**Before the appointment**
- Add your appointment date in the Appointments tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what could make them stronger.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most. Limit to three or four.
- Make your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Keep your medication list up to date.

**During the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can make the notes in that language.

**What these notes are, and what they are not**

These notes are a summary of what you entered, plus anything you chose to bring in from the Health app. These notes are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and any pattern in them is a coincidence check, not proof of cause. Your doctor may ask questions these notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication along with the start date. Within a few weeks, MenoMap can show your entries before and after, and this makes your next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a point in time: the day that marks 12 consecutive months without a period, when this is not caused by something else (such as pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but any age from the mid-40s to the mid-50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the period of some years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many changes associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin here, while periods still occur. Perimenopause can last a few years or much longer, and it differs for each person.

**Postmenopause** is the whole period after that 12-month mark. Some symptoms settle over time; others can continue for years.

Menopause can also happen earlier due to surgery that removes the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is identified.** For many people over 45, doctors identify perimenopause or menopause based on your history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. Such tests are more likely to be used when a person is younger or the picture is less clear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: flashes, sleep, mood and treatments, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a feeling of heat that comes on suddenly, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with skin flushing, sweating, a racing heart or a feeling of cold afterwards. Night sweats are the same thing during sleep, and they can be strong enough to wake you from sleep or soak your sheets.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people experience a few mild ones; others experience them many times a day to the point of disturbing work and sleep. For some people they settle within a few years; for others they continue much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many people notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, a hot room, stress or a thick blanket. These differ greatly between individuals, which is why tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes.** Skin flushing and sweating can also be caused by thyroid problems, infection, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or are accompanied by weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell your doctor.

**Describing them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- Roughly how many times a day and a night
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they disrupt: sleep, work, conversation, exercise
- What seems to happen beforehand
- What you have tried, and whether it changed anything

The Flash button and the after-the-fact log in MenoMap exist to record these accurately without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. The right choice for you should be discussed with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen that the body produces less of around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people, and it can also help other symptoms.

**It comes in various forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. People who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen along with estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the individual:** age, how long since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type and way the treatment is taken. That is why it is a decision to be made together with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions often asked:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- Which type and form does the doctor recommend, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and how quickly?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not getting treatment?
- What should I watch for, and when should we review it again?

**If you are already taking it,** record it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap will show your flashes before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not proof, so that you have something concrete to discuss at a review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing any medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people prefer other ways. There are several options.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence of reducing hot flashes. These include certain medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer class of medication designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapy and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence of making hot flashes and night sweats less disturbing and improving sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes found to help:**
- Layered clothing that can be removed quickly
- A fan on the desk and at the bedside
- A cooler bedroom and breathable sheets
- Identifying and reducing personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here)
- Regular physical activity and a regular sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal products.** The evidence for many of them is inconsistent or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medication. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about anything you take, including non-prescription products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiment compares your own entries before and during a change, and this is easier to judge than just a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember the nights across a month spontaneously. People tend to remember the most recent or the worst days. A simple record fills that gap.

**What the diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms happen and how strong, not just that they happen
- Whether things are getting better, getting worse or staying the same
- What happens around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medication
- A starting point to compare against if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary only helps if you keep it going. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Flash button and a four-question night check, so it only takes a few seconds, not a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Entries over two to four weeks usually show a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the most bothersome symptom, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. The Appointments tab in MenoMap helps you choose questions and print them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once you have not had a period for 12 months, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**, even if it happens only once, and even if it is only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time, the cause is not serious. For example, thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of something far easier to treat if found early. That is why public health guidance recommends having it checked rather than waiting.

**If you take hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns can be expected, depending on the type you take. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual, or that happens at the wrong time should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or health service and say that you have bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, how heavy it was, and anything else you notice. MenoMap can keep it for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It will remind you to have it checked and to include it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Disturbed sleep is one of the most common complaints in middle age, and it rarely has just one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too hot or damp to fall asleep again.

**Other common contributors:**
- Having to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but tends to fragment sleep in the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs, or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth raising, especially if you are very sleepy in the daytime)

**What usually helps.** A cool, dark room; breathable sheets and layered clothing that can be removed; a regular wake-up time; and reducing alcohol close to bedtime. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured approach that has been well studied, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What to track.** For a week or two, record your sleep score, night flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's night check and Flash log do this with a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app next to your night sweats, as context and not an explanation.

**When to have it checked.** Talk to a doctor if disturbed sleep affects your safety (for example, while driving), your mood, or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night.
